items.title: Prehistoric Predators: The Bizarre Biology of Terror Birds
items.description:
What kind of predator needs no teeth to terrify its prey? The terror birds were enormous flightless hunters that ruled South America for millions of years, standing metres tall and built for a life of pursuit and slaughter.

In this episode, Tristan Hughes is joined by palaeontologist Dr Steve Brusatte to explore the world of the phorusrhacids. What were these extraordinary birds really like? How did they dominate an isolated South America after the extinction of the dinosaurs? And what ultimate
items.why_watch: Palaeontologist Steve Brusatte joins the podcast to dig into the phorusrhacids — the giant, hook-beaked birds that dominated South American ecosystems for tens of millions of years without a single tooth. The conversation focuses on what their bone structure and fossil record actually tell us about how they hunted, rather than leaning on dramatized speculation. If you've ever wondered what apex predation looks like when it evolves in birds instead of mammals, this is a well-sourced, accessible answer.

items.why_watch: Artem Kirsanov, a Harvard neuroscience PhD student, grounds mind mapping in how memory and association actually work in the brain — so the advice feels earned rather than productivity-guru generic. At just eight minutes, the video covers both the cognitive rationale and specific software recommendations without padding. Worth it if you've tried mind maps before and weren't sure you were using them in a way that actually sticks.

global_silver_linings.title: Good-Humored Scientists Create ‘OnlyMarms’ Page to Boost Marmot Conservation and Donations
global_silver_linings.snippet: Desperate times call for desperate measures. With traditional funding sources facing cuts, The Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, which has spent the last 65 years studying yellow-bellied marmots, had to get creative. That soon led the Colorado researchers to the internet, where marmot videos have amassed millions of likes, with one especially hilarious Tik Tok video […] The post Good-Humored Scientists Create ‘OnlyMarms’ Page to Boost Marmot Conservation and Donations appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: A team of wildlife researchers is proving that conservation doesn't have to be dry or distant — by launching a playful, pun-named platform to draw public attention and funding to marmot protection. When scientists meet people where they are with warmth and wit, it opens doors that earnest appeals alone sometimes can't.
